entities.name: Sextus Quintilius Valerius Maximus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sextus Quintilius Valerius Maximus, a scion of the influential Quintilii family, was a prominent Roman senator and politician whose career spanned the reigns of emperors Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, and Commodus. Alongside his twin brother, Sextus Quintilius Condianus, he represented a pinnacle of senatorial power and intellectual prowess during the Pax Romana, embodying the ideal of the "philosopher-statesman" championed by Marcus Aurelius. His life and tragic death in 182 CE underscore the precarious nature of aristocratic influence under an increasingly autocratic imperial rule.

Maximus's distinguished career included a joint consulship with his brother in 151 CE, a rare honor that highlighted their familial prestige and shared political ascent. He served as governor of several key provinces, including Germania Inferior and Syria, where he would have commanded significant legions and managed complex administrative and military affairs on the empire's frontiers. His tenure in Syria, a strategically vital province, indicates the high trust placed in his administrative and military capabilities, contributing to the stability and defense of Rome's eastern borders during a period of potential Parthian threats.

The execution of Sextus Quintilius Valerius Maximus, along with his brother and son, on trumped-up charges of conspiracy against Emperor Commodus in 182 CE, marked a pivotal moment in Roman imperial history. This purge effectively extinguished one of Rome's most respected senatorial families, signaling Commodus's brutal consolidation of power and his disdain for the traditional senatorial elite. Their demise symbolized the end of the relative harmony between emperor and Senate that characterized the Antonine Age and ushered in a period of increased imperial tyranny and instability.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Sextus Quintilius Valerius Maximus's career exemplified the peak of senatorial influence under the Antonines, while his execution by Commodus marked a critical turning point in the relationship between emperor and Senate, signaling the end of an era of relative cooperation and the rise of imperial tyranny.
